passage: Sit, Abhinav. You asked why an old engineer like me still stays late on Thursdays. When I was twenty-five I had a good job at the pump factory, a scooter, my own desk by the window. I was content, truly. And still, every evening something itched. One day the watchman's son brought me his broken radio. I fixed it with him watching, explaining each wire, and his face lit up. So I started a Thursday class in the canteen for the workers' children. Then I had to learn more to answer their questions. Forty years later, I'm still learning. The day I think I've arrived, I'll stop being useful. That's Yusuf's rule, and now it can be yours.

passage: Deepak, twenty-five, loved his job at the city physiotherapy clinic, and he also felt it wasn't enough. So every Sunday he ran a free exercise class for older people in the temple hall. This Sunday the power went out and rain hammered the tin roof. The speaker for his music was dead, and half the chairs were wet. Twelve people had come anyway. Mahima, a nurse from his clinic, lit two lanterns and started clapping the rhythm. Deepak counted out the stretches loudly over the rain, laughing, adjusting each person's shoulder. On the bus home, soaked, he was already thinking about a balance course he wanted to take. There was always something more he could learn to help them better.

qa.q: How many people came to the class despite the rain?
qa.a: Twelve people had come anyway.

qa.q: What does Deepak thinking about a balance course on the bus suggest about his mood?
qa.a: It suggests he feels satisfied with the class yet restless to grow, always wanting to learn more so he can help better.

qa.q: Which choice kept the class going when the power failed?
qa.a: Deepak and Mahima improvised with lanterns, clapping and loud counting instead of cancelling, so the people who came still got their class.

qa.q: How might the older people in the hall see Deepak's Sunday class?
qa.a: They probably see it as something worth coming out for even in the rain, a warm space where someone skilled cares about their bodies.

grounding: A young professional uses his skills to serve others for free, feels content yet restless, and keeps looking to grow.

passage: Tenzin finished her last work call at seven and opened her laptop again on the balcony of her Bengaluru flat. Her day job building banking software paid well and she was good at it. Still, she'd been bored lately, restless in a way that a raise didn't fix. Downstairs, Binita Aunty was arguing with the colony secretary about the water tanker schedule again. Tenzin had been building a simple free web page where residents could see tanker timings and report leaks. Tonight she added a big-button version for older residents. At ten, Binita Aunty sent a voice note: "It works! Even I can use it 🙏" Tenzin smiled, then opened a tutorial on accessibility. There was so much she still didn't know.

passage:
"You're drawing shelves again?" Aparna asked, carrying two plates of curd rice to the table.
"Library shelves," Rukmini said, not looking up from her sketch. "For the government school near the bus depot. Low ones, so the little kids can reach."
"Don't you draw buildings all day at the firm?"
"Glass offices for people who already have everything." Rukmini finally put her pencil down. "I like my job, okay? I'm not unhappy. I just want my drawings to do something for someone."
"So you're happy and not happy."
"Exactly." Rukmini laughed. "Content and itchy."
"And when the shelves are done? Then you'll be satisfied?"
"Then the headmistress wants a reading corner. Then maybe a ramp for the side gate." She shrugged. "I don't think there's a finish line, Aparna. I think it just keeps going."
Aparna pushed a plate toward her. "Eat first. Then save the world."

qa.q: Where is the government school Rukmini is designing for?
qa.a: Near the bus depot.

qa.q: What does Rukmini mean when she calls herself 'content and itchy'?
qa.a: She is genuinely satisfied with her job but also restless, wanting her skills to help people who need them, not only clients who already have everything.

qa.q: What choice has Rukmini made with her skills, and how does she see where it leads?
qa.a: She uses her weekends to design shelves for the school, and she sees it as one step leading to the next, a reading corner, a ramp, rather than a finish line.

qa.q: How does Aparna see Rukmini's weekend project?
qa.a: Aparna is teasing but supportive, puzzled by 'happy and not happy', yet making sure Rukmini eats before she 'saves the world'.

grounding: It shows a young professional who feels both content and restless and uses her design skills to serve a school, seeing growth as ongoing rather than finished.

passage:
I'm Aparna. When I think back to last year, I remember how strange I felt. I was twenty-five, a sous chef at a good hotel in Pune. I liked my kitchen and my team. I was, honestly, content. But on my days off I'd feel this itch, as if something was waiting for me.
In June, my friend Rukmini, who coordinates a women's shelter, asked if I could teach one cooking class. I went on a Monday with a bag of vegetables and a borrowed tawa. Eight women, some shy, some bossy, and by the end they were calling me Didi. By the end we were arguing happily about how much chilli goes in poha.
That one class became every Monday. Two of the women now cook for a canteen.
I thought teaching would scratch the itch and that would be that. It didn't. Now I'm learning to teach better, and planning a baking month. It feels less like finishing and more like starting.

qa.q: What did Aparna carry to her first class?
qa.a: A bag of vegetables and a borrowed tawa.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel on her days off before she began teaching?
qa.a: She felt content with her work but restless, with an itch as if something was waiting for her.

qa.q: What turning point changed Aparna's year, and what came from it?
qa.a: Saying yes to Rukmini's request for one class turned into teaching every Monday, and two of the women now cook for a canteen.

qa.q: How might the women at the shelter experience Aparna's Monday classes?
qa.a: They may enjoy the lively, arguing kitchen, and for some the classes have led to real work cooking for a canteen.

grounding: It shows a young professional who is content yet restless, uses her cooking skills to teach women at a shelter and finds that growth keeps going rather than ending.
